summary: Correct park-bench layout and proportions, but flat bar end frames and untextured slats read as a simple CG prop.
critique: Overall proportions are plausible (about 1.8 m long, seat about 0.45 m, back about 0.85 m), with roughly 5 seat slats and 3 back slats. The end frames, which carry most of the character of a cast-iron bench, are plain constant-section rectangular bars: straight legs, a straight raked back post and a blocky L-shaped armrest that sticks out as a separate cap. There are no curves, scrolls, feet pads or casting draft, so from every angle it looks like extruded steel rather than cast iron. The back post rises well above the top back slat with a blunt square end. The slats are flat-coloured boxes with sharp edges: no bevels, no wood grain, no end-grain colour, no weathering, no visible screws or bolts where they meet the frames. The tan top/front slats and the dark shadowed slats look like two different materials. The frame is uniform matte dark grey with no paint wear or rust. The seat slats butt straight into the frames with no supporting cross-rail.
suggestions: Rebuild each end frame as one curved cast profile (about 30-40 verts outline, extruded 40-50 mm, about 150 tris per end): splayed front leg with a scroll foot, a back leg that sweeps up into a curved back support, and a rounded armrest that curls down into the front leg. This silhouette change matters most.
Bevel all slat edges (5 mm chamfer, 2 segments) and round the slat ends. Add a 50x50 mm seat cross-rail under the slats at each end and in the middle for 1.8 m+ benches.

Wood material: a tileable hardwood grain albedo (base about sRGB 120/85/55 for weathered teak, greying toward 140/130/115 on top faces), roughness 0.75-0.85, a slightly darker end-grain tint, and a vertex-colour or triplanar dirt gradient near the ends.
Add bolt heads (small 6-sided cylinders, 2 per slat per end, about 12 tris each, or a normal-map decal) where slats meet the frames.
Frame material: semi-gloss black or dark green enamel (roughness 0.4) with an edge-wear mask showing grey metal or rust on armrests and feet. Add a plaque decal on the top back slat for variety.
renderer_notes: The large brightness difference between sunlit and shaded slats comes from sun-only lighting with flat ambient, not from the asset.

summary: Reads as a smooth orange plastic dome; it is missing the flat brim, cut-outs and thin-shell look of a real disc marker.
critique: Real training disc cones are thin (about 1.5 mm) flexible PE shells, about 190-300 mm across and 50-75 mm tall. They have a pronounced flat or slightly flared brim at the base, a raised collar around the top hole, and usually 4 rectangular or rounded cut-outs in the side wall. This model is a solid-looking smooth frustum with a convex (bulging) profile and a rounded base edge, so it looks like a moulded clay pot or a pudding. The wall has no visible thickness at the top hole beyond a simple inset. There is no brim, no cut-outs, no moulding seam and no stacking ridges. The material is uniform matte orange with no plastic sheen, no translucency hint and no scuffs or grass stains. One detail view shows it as a very flat lens with no hole visible, which is inconsistent with the other views (either a framing issue or a non-uniform scale).
suggestions: Change the profile to a straight or slightly concave cone wall from about 0.62 radius up to a 0.22 radius top hole, with a 15-20 mm flat brim flaring out at the base. Lathe about 24-32 segments, about 200-300 tris total including a 1.5-2 mm wall thickness at the hole lip and brim edge.
Cut 4 evenly spaced side holes (about 35x25 mm, rounded corners). Geometry is fine at this size, or use an alpha-tested texture with a backface so the inside shows through.

Material: saturated orange (sRGB about 245/110/20), roughness 0.45, slight specular. Add a darker grass/mud smudge mask on the lower brim and a faint embossed brand ring on top as a normal-map detail.
Provide colour variants (yellow, red, blue, white) and a stacked variant (4-10 cones nested), since that is how they are usually seen on a training ground.
Check the scale against 190-300 mm diameter and 50-75 mm height. In the detail view the object looks closer to 300 mm and tall.
renderer_notes: The tall, blurred grass blades and the flat green band at the bottom of each tile come from the review framing and lawn, not the asset.

summary: A rounded grey box with a blank white front and a few fins; it is missing the yoke, LED optics and mounting that identify a sports LED floodlight.
critique: Modern stadium LED floodlights (Musco, Philips ArenaVision LED, Signify OptiVision) are dominated by a die-cast aluminium heatsink with many fine fins, a front lens array of dozens to hundreds of individual LED optics (often in visible modules with black louvres or glare visors), and a heavy U-shaped trunnion/yoke bracket with an aiming scale. This asset is a rounded-rectangle box with a flat featureless white front panel (it reads as an unlit lightbox or a whiteboard), about 7 thick, widely spaced plate fins on the back, and two small loose blocks at the ends that look detached rather than like a mounting bracket. There is no yoke, no pivot bolt, no visor, no driver box, no cable gland and no lens detail. The side view shows a stepped black block that does not read as any real luminaire. The aspect ratio (about 3:1, long and low) is plausible for a linear module, but nothing else confirms the identity.
suggestions: Front face: replace the white slab with a recessed lens panel showing a grid of LED optics. Use a normal/emissive texture (for example 6x16 circular lenses on a 512x256 texture) behind a 15-20 mm deep black bezel. Add an emissive mask so it lights up in night scenes. Geometry cost is about 0 extra; a 256-512 px texture is enough.
Add a U-shaped yoke: two 10 mm thick side plates (trapezoid profile) running to a rear mounting plate, with pivot discs (16-sided cylinders) where they meet the housing. About 150-250 tris.
Back: use 20-30 thin fins (about 3-4 mm, close pitch) and alpha-cut or normal-map the in-between spacing to keep tris low, or bake the fin detail into a normal map on 4-6 actual fins.
Add an asymmetric glare visor / top hood (a bent plate over the top 30% of the face, about 20 tris), a small driver box on the back, and a cable gland.

Material: housing in powder-coated grey (sRGB about 110/112/115, roughness 0.5) with slight dirt streaks from the fins downward. Lens area: dark glass (roughness 0.1) over bright LED dots. Remove the plain white albedo.
renderer_notes: No reflections are available, so a real lens would also look flat here; an emissive or normal-mapped lens grid is needed to read in this viewer.

summary: Correct mini-goal frame and proportions, but the net reads as a rigid welded wire panel instead of soft netting.
critique: The tubular frame is good: rounded bends at the top corners, ground bars, rear angled side struts, and a plausible 1.5 x 1 m mouth with about 0.8 m depth. The main realism break is the net. It is a perfectly flat, perfectly regular square grid with thick, uniform strands that stay straight in every panel, with no sag, no billow at the back, and no lacing to the frame. In several views (especially the side and the opposite three-quarter) it looks like a steel mesh fence panel rather than polyethylene netting. The cords are drawn too thick for their spacing (about 100 mm mesh with roughly 6-8 mm visible cords). The frame has no welds, end caps, joints, net clips/hooks or ground pegs. The white paint has no scuffs, grass staining near the ground or chipped edges. The lower rear bar meets the ground with no anchoring.
suggestions: Net shape: displace the net mesh vertices so the back and roof panels sag 50-100 mm between frame members (a simple catenary or parabola per panel) and the bottom edge lies slack on the ground in a few loose folds. Keep the frame straight. This is cheap and the biggest single fix.

Use an alpha-tested net texture on a few quads per panel instead of geometry strands. A 256 px tile with knotted 3 mm cords at 100 mm (or 120 mm hex) mesh costs about 2 tris per panel and reads correctly at all distances. Keep anti-aliased cords like the main goal.
Add net clips: small white or grey loop rings every 150-200 mm along the frame (instanced, about 8 tris each), or a normal-mapped lacing strip.
Frame: add end caps on the ground bars, small weld beads or sleeve joints at the corners, and two U-shaped ground pegs at the back corners.

Material: frame white powder coat (sRGB about 235, roughness 0.35) with a grass-green/mud gradient on the bottom 100 mm and a few chipped edges showing grey steel. Net: off-white polyethylene, roughness 0.8, slightly translucent.
renderer_notes: The grey cast on the frame and net in the shaded views comes from sun-only lighting plus flat sky ambient.

summary: Recognisable as a green ride-on mower, but built from blocky primitives with clipping tyres, a slab seat and no hood detail.
critique: Colour scheme and layout (front hood, mid deck, rear seat over large rear wheels) read as a John Deere-style lawn tractor, but construction is toy-like. The hood is a simple chamfered box with no grille, headlights, vent slots, badge or tapered nose. The seat is two flat slabs (a base and a tall rectangular back) with no cushion shape, high-back contour or armrests, and the back is far taller than a real X350 seat. The rear fenders are small flat pads, and the rear tyre lugs visibly poke through them (clipping in the close-up). The deck is a flat dark slab with no rounded shell, discharge chute or deck wheels. The steering column is a bare stick with no dash panel, fuel cap, levers or pedals. There is no frame or chassis visible between the wheels, and there are no footrests or running boards. The rear wheels look only slightly larger than the front; on a real X350 the rears are about 20 in and the fronts about 15 in. Overall length looks short for about 1.8-2.4 m. Materials are flat untextured green, black and yellow with no gloss variation, decals or dirt.
suggestions: Fix the clipping: raise the rear fenders or enlarge them into proper curved wheel arches (a half-tube at about 0.6x tyre width), wrapping about 110 degrees over each rear tyre.

Hood: taper the nose (narrower and lower at the front), add a black mesh grille insert on the front face, two rectangular headlights, side vent slots (normal map) and a yellow stripe/decal. About 300-500 tris more.
Seat: model a contoured moulded seat (a dished pan with a rounded 350 mm-high back, about 200 tris) in black vinyl (roughness 0.55), mounted on a spring bracket.
Wheels: rear about 510 mm, front about 380 mm diameter. Keep the yellow rims, add a turf-tread pattern via normal map rather than spiky lugs (real turf tyres have shallow chevrons).

Add an operator platform/footrests, a dash panel with a key and throttle lever, a fuel cap behind the hood, a side discharge chute on the deck, small deck anti-scalp wheels, and a tow hitch at the rear.
Materials: glossy John Deere-like green paint (roughness 0.3, clearcoat feel), satin black plastics, grass clippings and dust mask on the deck and lower body.

summary: A clean box with a slab roof and flat dark window panels; it reads as greybox-plus rather than a real GRP or steel gatehouse.
critique: Prefabricated security kiosks are about 1.5-2.5 m square with GRP or steel-panel walls showing vertical panel seams or ribs, aluminium-framed windows with mullions and sills, a door with handle, hinges and kick plate, a small canopy or gutter, and service details (AC unit, light, CCTV, cable entry, lifting points, base skid). This asset has smooth seamless white walls with rounded vertical corners. The windows are flat dark-blue or black panels inset with a thin grey frame, with no glazing bars, sills, reflections or interior. The door is a flat grey rectangle with no handle, hinges, frame or glazing. The roof is a uniform dark slab with a rounded-corner overhang, with no fascia, gutter or downpipe. The SECURITY sign is a nice touch but reads as a sticker. There is no base or plinth, so the walls meet the grass with no skirting. The back window renders pure black, which reads as a hole.
suggestions: Glazing: give windows a 40-50 mm aluminium frame with one vertical or horizontal mullion, a protruding sill (30 mm), and glass with a simple interior cue: either an interior-mapping/parallax texture (desk, chair, monitor glow) or a darkened room box behind semi-transparent glass. This is the biggest realism gain, at about 100 tris + a 512 px interior texture.
Walls: add vertical panel seams every 600-1000 mm (normal map or 5 mm grooves), a 150 mm skirting/plinth on a raised base, and slight dirt streaking below the windows and roof edge.
Door: add a frame, lever handle, 3 hinges, kick plate and optionally a vision panel. Add a step or ramp in front.

Roof: add a fascia edge with a drip line, a gutter and a downpipe at one corner. Add a wall-mounted AC condenser, a bulkhead light over the door, and a small CCTV camera on a corner bracket (each 50-150 tris).
Materials: GRP walls off-white (sRGB about 225/225/218, roughness 0.5) with a faint orange-peel normal. Roof membrane dark grey, roughness 0.8. Make the sign a raised plate with screws.
renderer_notes: The lack of screen-space reflections makes any glass look flat; window glass needs a baked reflection/interior texture to read in this viewer.

summary: Convincing Norway spruce silhouette with drooping branches, let down by a bright tuft at the apex, an over-exposed pink trunk and flat dark foliage cards.
critique: The silhouette is the strongest part. It has a narrow conical crown with branches that droop and then sweep up at the tips (typical of a mature Picea abies), the branches are spaced in plausible whorls, and the cast shadow is detailed and believable. Problems: (1) the leader at the very top ends in a lighter, rounder green blob that looks like a different asset stuck on and breaks the spire tip a spruce should have. (2) The trunk is visible through almost the entire crown and is a pale pinkish-tan with a bright lit stripe. Real spruce bark is grey-brown to reddish-brown and mostly hidden by dense foliage in the upper crown. Here the branch structure looks like bare pink sticks with foliage clumps hanging off them. (3) Foliage is a uniform very dark green with little value variation: no lighter new-growth tips, no translucency, no ambient-occlusion gradient from outer to inner crown. Cards are visible as flat clumps when viewed from above. (4) The crown is somewhat sparse and see-through compared to a healthy spruce, which is nearly opaque. (5) The lowest branches start very close to the ground. That is fine for an open-grown tree, but there is no root flare or ground litter.
suggestions: Replace the apex blob with a thin tapering leader (about 0.5-1 m) and 3-5 small upward-angled top branches with foliage cards, matching the rest of the crown colour.

Increase foliage density in the upper two-thirds, about 30-50% more cards, so the trunk is mostly hidden. Keep the total at about 3-6k tris for the hero LOD by using larger cards with a denser alpha texture.
Bark: grey-brown (sRGB about 95/80/70) with a scaly normal map. Darken branch wood under the foliage via vertex AO so the inner branches stop reading as bright pink sticks.

Foliage shading: vertex-colour AO from trunk to outer shell (inner 40% darker), lighter yellow-green tips on the outer 10-15% of cards, and a cheap backlit translucency term. Vary hue slightly per branch.
Add a slight root flare at the base (6-8 extra verts ring) and a needle-litter ground decal under the crown. Also provide a billboard/impostor LOD.
renderer_notes: No GI means the inner crown is not darkened naturally; baked vertex AO is required in this viewer.

summary: Strong two-tier bowl with individual seats, aisles and vomitories; it is let down by uniform flat-red seats and missing rails and edge details.
critique: The bowl reads well. Individual tip-up seats are geometrically present, row rake and aisle stairs are plausible, the lower and upper tiers are separated by a fascia, and vomitory openings with stairs are cut into the seating. Close up it starts to look CG: every seat is the same saturated red with no colour variation, fading or numbering. The vomitories are dark rectangular pits with no handrails, safety glass or barrier walls. Aisles have no handrails or step nosings (yellow edges). The front of the lower tier sits on a plain dark wall with no barrier or glazing. Seat backs show strong moire at distance. Upper tier seats in shadow go nearly black-red.
suggestions: Add handrails along aisles and around every vomitory (a 40 mm tube at 1.1 m, instanced segments) and a glass or steel balustrade on the front of each tier.

Seat material: slight per-seat hue/value jitter (+/-5%) via instance colour, a fade gradient toward sun-exposed rows, and seat-number decals on backs. Optionally add a pattern (club name or crest spelled in a contrasting seat colour), which is common in Premier League grounds.
Paint step nosings yellow or white on aisle stairs (a vertex colour on the riser edge) and add row-letter plates on the aisle ends.
Use a distance LOD where the seat rows become a normal-mapped tiered strip to cut moire and triangle count.
renderer_notes: The near-black upper tiers in the opposite three-quarter view come from the lack of GI/sky occlusion under the roof, which needs a fill or baked AO, not an asset change.

summary: Underside shows a credible truss and purlin grid with translucent panels, but the leading edge is thin and the roof top is a featureless black slab.
critique: From inside, the roof underside has radial trusses, purlins and a lighter translucent zone near the leading edge, plus a white band suggesting a lighting gantry. This reads like a modern cantilever roof. However the members are all the same thin gauge with no hierarchy (primary trusses should be much deeper than purlins), there are no catwalks, speaker clusters or cable trays, and the cladding is a flat grey with no panel seams. In the exterior view the roof top is a single unbroken black surface with no ribs, gutters, translucent strip or edge fascia, so it reads as a flat cap.
suggestions: Give primary trusses real depth (1.5-3 m triangular or Warren truss) with lighter secondary purlins between them, and add a catwalk with handrail along the leading edge.
Add a leading-edge fascia/gutter (0.5-1 m deep) and speaker clusters/floodlight rows hung from it.
Roof top: standing-seam metal normal map with a lighter translucent polycarbonate band at the inner edge, plus drainage gutters and a few maintenance walkways.
Add panel joints and a slight value variation to the underside cladding.
renderer_notes: The pure-black roof top in the night exterior view may be lighting (no moon or ambient), so check it in a day render before changing the material.

summary: A bold Allianz-style glowing red diamond skin with dark columns, but no entrances, stairs or ground-level detail, and it is mostly lost in darkness.
critique: The idea of an illuminated cushion or diamond skin is clear and the curved bowl reads, but the facade is a uniform red emissive surface with a regular diamond wireframe. It has no inflated-pillow shading, no frame mullions or depth, and no unlit or darker panels. The columns are plain black boxes. There are no turnstile entrances, stair cores, concourse openings, signage, club crest or ground-plane plaza. Everything that is not emissive renders black, so the massing above and below the skin can't be judged.
suggestions: Model the skin as shallow pillows (each diamond slightly domed, or normal-mapped) with metallic frame members of real width (100-150 mm), and vary emissive intensity per panel (+/-10%).
Add ground-level elements: turnstile blocks with numbered gates, glazed concourse entrances, stair/ramp cores, a club name on the facade, and a plaza with paving.
Give the columns a tapered or articulated profile with base plates.
Provide a day material state (non-emissive white/translucent skin) so the asset works in daytime scenes.
renderer_notes: The exterior is shown at night with no ambient, so most of the structure is pure black; a day or dusk view is needed to judge it fairly.

summary: The only floodlighting visible is a plain white band on the roof leading edge, with no individual luminaires.
critique: Premier League grounds use rows of individual LED floodlights mounted on a gantry along the roof leading edge, which is clearly visible from the stands. In these views there is just a continuous bright strip under the roof edge, with no fixtures, aiming angles or gantry structure. At this distance the band reads as a strip light rather than a sports lighting rig.
suggestions: Instance the floodlight_fixture.led asset (once improved) in rows of 40-80 per side on a catwalk gantry along the roof leading edge, each aimed at the pitch with slightly varied tilt.
Add the gantry: a 1 m-deep truss with handrail, cable trays and access ladders.
Add an emissive lens state for night matches and light the pitch accordingly.
renderer_notes: The floodlights could not be fully assessed from these views; they may be more visible in the overall sheet.

summary: Clean mowing stripes and crisp lines; at player height the turf is flat colour and the goals are not shown in this sheet.
critique: Mowing stripes, the halfway line, the touchline, corner flag and technical-area markings are all present and correctly proportioned. From the low camera the turf is a flat gradient with no blade texture, no wear near the goalmouths or technical area, and the lines are perfectly uniform. The run-off area colour matches the pitch exactly. Goals and nets are not visible in this detail sheet, so they can't be scored here.
suggestions: Add a detail-normal/albedo grass texture that fades in under about 20 m, and a wear mask (goalmouths, centre circle, linesman runs, warm-up zone in front of the dugouts).
Give lines a slight soft edge and value noise (painted-on-grass look).
Differentiate the run-off strip (slightly different shade or artificial turf) and add pitch-side drainage or sprinkler heads.
renderer_notes: The grass blades in other sheets are the viewer lawn; inside the stadium the pitch shader is in use.

summary: Believable extendable tunnel and padded dugout seats, but the canopies and tunnel ribs are simple and lack hardware.
critique: The telescopic tunnel (red fabric arches) and the rows of grey bucket seats in the dugouts read correctly. The central tunnel mouth in the stand has a lit arch frame. But the tunnel fabric is smooth with no folds or fabric seams, and the ribs are plain thin arcs. The dugout canopies are barely visible thin frames with no polycarbonate shell, branding or side panels. There are no technical-area props (fourth official board, water bottles, coolers, kit bags). The tunnel mouth is an untextured black void.
suggestions: Model the dugout as a curved clear polycarbonate shell (slight tint, roughness 0.1) on a steel frame with a branded fascia strip and side wind panels.
Tunnel: add fabric sag between ribs (scallop the canopy geometry), seam lines, the club crest or sponsor print on the sides, and wheels or feet at the base of each rib.
Give the stadium tunnel mouth some interior depth (walls, lights, a gradient instead of pure black).
Add instanced props: drinks crates, cool boxes, bottle carriers and a 4th-official table.

summary: Tier-fascia LED ribbons with varied fictional sponsors look good, but the pitch-side boards are mostly blank grey slabs.
critique: The ribbon boards on the tier fascias are the strongest advertising element. They have varied, legible fictional brands (Kestrel Bank, Halcyon, Volta, Summit Cola), believable layouts and colour blocks. The perimeter boards at pitch level, which are the most prominent at camera height, show as grey and white slabs with only a small logo stripe. They have no LED pixel content, no frame, no back struts and no padding top. The big screen is only visible as a speck in the exterior view. Emissive brightness is the same across all panels, with no LED pixel structure up close.
suggestions: Fill the pitch-side LED boards with the same sponsor content as the ribbons (sharper, larger logos), with an emissive boost of about 1.5x relative to diffuse and a fine LED pixel grid normal or albedo pattern visible under 10 m.
Model the board housing: a slanted black front frame, rear support legs and a foam top pad (about 50 tris per 2 m segment).
Add 3D carpets or advertising mats behind the goals, and make the main screen visible from the stands, with a frame, a back structure and live score content.
renderer_notes: The pitch-side boards may be rendered unlit or with a placeholder texture in this layout; check that the material assignment is actually reaching them.
